titleStmt.title: The Cascade Equivalence Hypothesis: When Do Speech LLMs Behave Like ASR→LLM Pipelines?

analytic.title: The Cascade Equivalence Hypothesis: When Do Speech LLMs Behave Like ASR→LLM Pipelines?

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Current speech LLMs largely perform implicit ASR: on tasks solvable from a transcript, they are behaviorally and mechanistically equivalent to simple Whisper→LLM cascades. We show this through matched-backbone testing across four speech LLMs and six tasks, controlling for the LLM backbone for the first time. Ultravox is statistically indistinguishable from its matched cascade (κ=0.93); logit lens reveals literal text emerging in hidden states; LEACE concept erasure confirms text representations are causally necessary in both architectures tested, collapsing accuracy to near-zero. Qwen2-Audio genuinely diverges, revealing cascade equivalence is architecturedependent, not universal. For most deployed use cases, current speech LLMs are expensive cascades, and under noise, they are worse ones, with clean-condition advantages reversing by up to 7.6% at 0 dB.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: End-to-end speech large language models (speech LLMs) such as Qwen2-Audio [1], Ultravox [2], Phi-4-Multimodal [3], and Gemini [4] accept audio directly and produce text responses, bypassing the traditional pipeline of automatic speech recognition followed by a text LLM. The implicit promise is richer understanding: by processing raw audio, these models should capture paralinguistic cues (prosody, emotion, emphasis) that ASR discards. This promise has driven substantial investment across diverse architectures, from discrete audio tokens [5] to learned connectors [2] to cross-attention [1] to dual encoders [6], yet whether this diversity translates to genuinely different internal processing remains untested.

But does this promise hold? On tasks that can be solved from a transcript alone (factual question answering, topic classification, sentiment analysis), do speech LLMs actually exploit acoustic information beyond what a simple Whisper-to-LLM cascade provides? Or do they converge on implicit text representations, effectively becoming cascades with extra steps?

Prior work offers fragments of an answer. LISTEN [7] showed speech LLMs rely on lexical cues even for emotion recognition, but tested only emotion tasks without cascade comparison or per-example error analysis. SALAD [8] measured the speech-text understanding gap within models but analyzed only aggregate accuracy, not whether speech and cascade pathways fail on the same examples in the same ways; critically, comparing speech vs. text input to a single model tests in-put robustness, not architectural equivalence. Broader benchmarks [9,10] also report only aggregate performance. Separately, Cuervo and Marxer [11] showed speech LLMs scale orders of magnitude less efficiently than text LLMs, raising the question of whether end-to-end speech processing is worth the investment when a cascade might suffice. The evaluation studies above share two limitations, to varying degrees. First, none analyzes per-example behavioral agreement (whether two systems produce the same answer on the same input), which is necessary to distinguish genuine architectural divergence from superficially similar accuracy. Second, cross-model comparisons (benchmarks, LISTEN) do not control for the LLM backbone. When Qwen2-Audio (built on Qwen2-7B) is compared against a Whisper + Qwen2.5-7B cascade, any observed difference conflates the speech processing architecture with the different reasoning capabilities of the underlying LLM. A model might appear to "diverge from its cascade" simply because its backbone reasons differently, not because it processes audio differently.

We introduce matched-backbone behavioral testing to resolve this confound. By constructing cascades that pair Whisper with the same LLM backbone used inside each speech LLM (Llama-3.1-8B for Ultravox, Qwen2-7B for Qwen2-Audio, Phi-4-mini for Phi-4-Multimodal), we isolate architectural effects from backbone effects. This reveals that the backbone confound can inflate apparent architectural divergence by up to +0.13 κ, closing much of the gap toward the cascade ceiling.

We formalize the underlying question as the Cascade Equivalence Hypothesis: on tasks where the transcript is informationally sufficient, i.e., I(A; Y | T ) ≈ 0 with A the audio, T the transcript, and Y the task label, a speech LLM should be behaviorally indistinguishable from a cascade using the same LLM backbone. We test this not through aggregate accuracy, which can mask disagreement at the example level, but through per-example behavioral metrics: Cohen's κ [12] for agreement, conditional error overlap for shared failure modes, and McNemar's test [13] for systematic directional bias.

Our results establish cascade equivalence as a spectrum across architectures, with mechanistic evidence explaining why. We detail our methodology ( §2-3), behavioral findings ( §4), mechanistic evidence ( §5), and implications ( §6-7). Our contributions are:

div.head: The Cascade Equivalence Hypothesis
div.p: Consider a spoken input A, its transcript T = ASR(A), and a task label Y . We define the acoustic surplus for task Y as:

When ∆IY ≈ 0, the transcript preserves nearly all task-relevant information; we call such tasks text-sufficient (e.g., factual QA, topic classification, sentiment analysis). Tasks whose labels depend on prosodic cues that transcription discards, such as emotion recognition and sarcasm detection, are text-insufficient.

Text sufficiency is a property of the (task, ASR system) pair: what matters is whether a realistic ASR transcript, with its characteristic errors, preserves enough information for the downstream task. Billa [14] demonstrated this empirically, showing that even high-WER ASR transcripts in mismatched languages preserve enough structural regularity for downstream performance improvements.

When ∆IY ≈ 0, the transcript carries all task-relevant information, so any system that extracts T from A-whether an explicit ASR module or a learned internal representationwill support the same downstream predictions. We call this the Cascade Equivalence Hypothesis: on text-sufficient tasks (I(A; Y | T ) ≈ 0), a speech LLM should be behaviorally indistinguishable from a cascade using the same LLM backbone. The matched-backbone requirement is critical; without it, behavioral differences may reflect the reasoning capabilities of different LLMs rather than different audio processing.

This hypothesis has testable implications at two levels. Behaviorally, a speech LLM and its matched-backbone cascade should exhibit high per-example agreement on text-sufficient tasks, with agreement decreasing on text-insufficient tasks if acoustic surplus is exploited; when both systems err, they should produce the same wrong answer at rates above chance, the signature of a shared reasoning pathway. Mechanistically, internal representations should progressively converge toward text, and erasing the text-predictive subspace should collapse task performance, confirming that text representations are causally necessary rather than epiphenomenal.

div.head: Systems Under Test
div.p: We evaluate four end-to-end speech LLMs and five ASR→LLM cascades (Table 1). All cascades use Whisperlarge-v3 [15] for ASR. Three "matched-backbone" cascades pair Whisper with the same LLM backbone used inside each open-weight speech LLM: Qwen2-7B [16] for Qwen2-Audio, Llama-3.1-8B [17] for Ultravox, and Phi-4-mini for Phi-4-Multimodal. Two additional cascades, "strong" (Whisper-large → Qwen2.5-7B) and "weak" (Whispersmall → Qwen2.5-7B), provide upper and lower reference points. Total: 6,300 evaluation samples, 27,300 audio files. Noise perturbation conditions (multi-talker babble at 15, 10, 5, and 0 dB SNR using MUSAN [24]) are applied to two TTS voices across the text-sufficient tasks.

div.head: Behavioral Metrics
div.p: For each (speech LLM, cascade) pair on each classification task, we compute: Cohen's κ, chance-corrected per-example agreement; conditional error overlap, P (same wrong answer | both wrong), testing shared failure mechanisms; and Mc-Nemar's test, whether one system is systematically better (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-corrected across all pair×task comparisons).

div.head: Probing and Intervention
div.p: For the two open-weight speech LLMs (Qwen2-Audio, Ultravox) plus Whisper as a control, we extract hidden states at nine layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 31}) on 1,000 utterances and train: acoustic probes, linear regression for energy (R 2 ) and pitch (R 2 ); text probes: a CTC probe, a perframe linear classifier trained with CTC loss to decode character sequences from hidden states, scored by text decodability (1-CER, where higher values indicate more decodable text); and a bag-of-characters (BoC) probe (linear regression on character frequency vectors, R 2 ). This linear probing methodology [25] is standard for high-dimensional representations (d≈4096, n≈800). Logit lens [26] projects hidden states at audio positions through the LLM's own unembedding matrix at each layer. Following standard practice for pre-norm architectures [27], we apply the model's final RMSNorm to intermediate hidden states before projecting through the unembedding matrix, ensuring that the scale and distribution of hidden states match what the language modeling head expects. If top-predicted tokens resolve to transcript words, the model is literally converting audio to text internally. For Ultravox, we project only audio token positions (identified per-utterance); for Qwen2-Audio (cross-attention architecture), all positions are projected. AudioLens [28] recently applied similar projection to audio-language models for attribute recognition; we apply the technique to study text emergence in speech LLMs. LEACE concept erasure [29] provides causal evidence by surgically removing specific information from the model's representations during inference. We use the concept-erasure library2 to compute optimal linear erasers from hidden states and concept labels at each layer. If the model relies on text information for its predictions, erasing the text-predictive directions should collapse performance; if it does not, erasure should have no effect. We apply erasure at all nine probed layers simultaneously on every forward pass, including during autoregressive generation, so the model cannot recover the erased information from unmodified layers [30,31]. We disable bias centering (use bias=False) because the training mean, computed from audio-token hidden states, is out-of-distribution for text tokens generated during decoding, causing model collapse when applied. We test five erasure conditions spanning a gradient of text specificity: BoC erasure fits LEACE on character frequency vectors (48-dimensional concept); proxy erasure fits LEACE on first-word classification labels (159-dimensional concept); CTC erasure fits LEACE on per-frame character predictions from the trained CTC probe (49-class concept, capturing sequential character order). Two controls complete the design: random erasure removes a random 159-dimensional orthogonal subspace as a dimensionality-matched control; acoustic erasure fits LEACE on pitch and energy values (2-dimensional concept).

div.head: Agreement on Text-Sufficient Tasks
div.p: Table 2 presents accuracy and Figure 1 shows matchedbackbone κ for all systems.

Ultravox is near-cascade-equivalent. Against its matched Llama-3.1-8B cascade, Ultravox achieves κ = 0.93 [0.92, 0.94] on AG News, 0.78 [0.76, 0.79] on CSQA, and 0.75 [0.74, 0.77] on SST-2. On CSQA, McNemar's test is non-significant after FDR correction (p = 0.29): the systems make errors at statistically indistinguishable rates. The CSQA κ jumps from 0.65 (against the mismatched Cascade-S) to 0.78 with the matched backbone, a +0.13 increase that closes much of the gap toward the cascade ceiling (0.96).

Qwen2-Audio genuinely diverges. Even against its own Qwen2-7B backbone cascade, κ on text-sufficient tasks remains moderate (0.54-0.85) and shows minimal improvement over the mismatched comparison. On SST-2, κ actually decreases from 0.62 to 0.54. Qwen2-Audio processes sentiment through a pathway that is architecturally distinct from any cascade.

The cascade-S vs. cascade-W ceiling validates this taxonomy: κ = 0.93-0.98 despite a substantial ASR quality gap, confirming that even degraded transcripts carry nearly all taskrelevant information. Phi-4-MM and Gemini fall between these extremes, establishing that cascade equivalence is a spectrum rather than a binary property (Figure 1). Phi-4-MM's Mixtureof-LoRAs architecture achieves κ=0.85 on AG News (matching Qwen2-Audio) but only 0.23 on MELD, the lowest of any matched pair. Combined with its low MELD accuracy (30.2%, Table 2), this indicates that Phi-4-MM neither follows the cascade text pathway nor exploits paralinguistic cues effectively; its modality routing mechanism appears to discard emotionrelevant acoustic information without replacing it.

div.head: Shared Error Signatures
div.p: The clearest evidence for cascade equivalence is not shared accuracy but shared failures. On AG News, 81% of joint errors between Ultravox and its matched cascade occur despite correct transcription: both systems understood the audio perfectly but failed at the same classification boundary. The speech pathway contributed nothing; the failures originate entirely in shared LLM reasoning.

Quantitatively, conditional error overlap (P (same wrong answer | both wrong)) reaches 0.96 on AG News, 0.85 on CSQA, and 0.68 on MELD, representing 2.9-4.1× chance baselines (Figure 2). For binary tasks (SST-2), conditional error overlap is uninformative since only one wrong answer exists; we report overlap ratios for multi-class tasks only.

Table 3 illustrates representative shared failures. Across multi-class tasks, 84-96% of joint errors involve the identical wrong label, far above the 17-33% chance baselines. Two mechanisms emerge: LLM reasoning errors, where both systems decode correctly but fail at the same classification boundary (e.g., tech-company stories classified as Business), and ASR-induced errors, where identical transcription failures cause identical downstream failures (e.g., "mountie" misrecognized as "Amante," destroying the Canada clue). On SST-2, 66% of shared errors involve a degraded transcript, consistent with sentiment's sensitivity to single words (negations, intensifiers).

div.head: Text-Insufficient Tasks
div.p: On MELD and MUStARD, κ drops substantially for all pairs (Figure 1), as the cascade equivalence hypothesis predicts for text-insufficient tasks. However, the matched-backbone analysis reveals that the backbone confound accounts for a substantial portion of this gap. Ultravox's MELD κ improves from 0.40 (vs. Cascade-S) to 0.52 (vs. its matched cascade); MUStARD from 0.25 to 0.55. The backbone confound is thus substantial even on text-insufficient tasks, reinforcing that matched-backbone comparison is essential. The matched κ values (∼0.5) are well below the text-sufficient ceiling (0.93- Qwen2-Audio shows minimal change from backbone matching: MELD κ moves from 0.37 to 0.30, and MUStARD from 0.05 to 0.05. This is perhaps expected given that the mismatched (Qwen2.5-7B) and matched (Qwen2-7B) backbones share the same Qwen lineage. MUStARD κ ≈ 0.05 (near zero) indicates either genuine exploitation of paralinguistic features or a qualitatively different processing strategy. Since Qwen2-Audio's MUStARD accuracy (52.8%) barely exceeds chance, a different but not better strategy is more likely.

div.head: Noise Robustness
div.p: Under multi-talker babble noise (MUSAN, 0-15 dB SNR), our Whisper-based cascades degrade substantially less than the E2E models tested. At 0 dB, Cascade-S loses 0.5-4.2% accuracy across text-sufficient tasks, while E2E models show substantially larger drops on SST-2 and CSQA (5.9-12.7%; Figure 3). This asymmetry is expected: Whisper, trained on 680,000 hours of diverse audio, acts as a noise-robust front-end that absorbs acoustic degradation before it reaches the LLM.

Gemini degrades fastest despite the best clean accuracy: SST-2 drops 10.2% at 0 dB (90.4% → 80.3%) vs. Cascade-S's 2.6% drop. This means that selecting a system based on cleancondition accuracy can reverse under deployment noise: a team choosing Gemini over Cascade-S for SST-2 would see a 7.6 percentage-point reversal at 0 dB (from +2.0% clean advantage to -5.6% disadvantage), invisible in standard benchmarks.

div.head: Mechanistic Evidence
div.p: We now move from behavioral observation to mechanistic analysis, building a four-level case: what is encoded (probing), how it emerges (logit lens), whether the emergent text carries task-relevant information (functional text test), and whether it is causally necessary (LEACE erasure). Left axis: acoustic probe R 2 for energy (solid, circles) and pitch (dashed, squares). Right axis: CTC text decodability (solid, triangles) and bag-of-characters R 2 (dashed, diamonds). Qwen2-Audio shows the strongest acoustic compression; Ultravox retains acoustics while building text representations.

div.head: Layer-wise Probing
div.p: Figure 4 shows acoustic and text probe results across layers for Qwen2-Audio, Ultravox, and Whisper. Whisper serves as a control: as a dedicated ASR encoder, it provides a reference for how a model that is explicitly trained to convert speech to text organizes acoustic and textual information across layers. Whisper's CTC text decodability shows a non-monotonic pattern, dipping to 0.16 at layer 16 before recovering to 0.26 by layer 31, consistent with an encoder bottleneck where midlayers focus on acoustic processing and later layers build text representations.

Acoustic information is retained but restructured. Energy R 2 remains high throughout: 0.92 → 0.86 for Qwen2-Audio, 0.86 → 0.83 for Ultravox, and 0.99 → 0.96 for Whisper. However, pitch R 2 declines more steeply (Qwen2-Audio: 0.63 → 0.48; Ultravox: 0.37 → 0.31), suggesting finer-grained acoustic features are progressively overwritten as the model builds text representations.

Text decodability reveals divergent architectures. Ultravox shows progressive text emergence (CTC: 0.03 → 0.20), while Qwen2-Audio maintains stable text decodability (0.48-0.51) through layers 0-20 before a sharp decline in the final layers (0.43 at L24, 0.29 at L31); its cross-attention encoder already produces text-rich representations that the LLM reorganizes in its final layers rather than building from scratch. This inversion reveals that Qwen2-Audio's encoder has already solved the speech-to-text problem before the LLM layers begin; the LLM's role is not to build text but to reason over it, mirroring a cascade's division of labor.

The acoustic compression gradient maps onto behavioral agreement: Qwen2-Audio (steepest pitch decline, 0.63 → 0.48) shows the lowest κ with its cascade; Ultravox (milder decline, 0.37 → 0.31) shows higher κ. Table 4 reports exact values at key layers.

div.head: Logit Lens: Visualizing Text Emergence
div.p: While probing requires an external classifier, the logit lens [26,27] reveals text emergence through the model's own unembedding matrix, requiring no training. Figure 5 and Table 5 show bag-of-tokens precision (fraction of greedily decoded tokens appearing in the reference transcript) by layer.

Both models build text representations, but the degree differs markedly. Ultravox reaches 0.34 bag precision at layer 31 with recognizable paraphrases (e.g., "the House of Commons in July" for a reference containing "House of Commons on April 27th 1992"). Qwen2-Audio peaks at 0.23 (layer 28) with fragmented, multilingual output bearing artifacts from Qwen2's vocabulary. This 55% gap in text emergence mirrors the behav- The degree of text emergence mirrors the behavioral agreement spectrum.

div.head: Is the Emergent Text Behaviorally Sufficient?
div.p: The logit lens shows text emerging at audio positions in Ultravox by layer 31. But is this text merely a byproduct of processing, or does it carry the information that drives the model's predictions? We test this for Ultravox by extracting the text visible at layer 31 via logit lens decoding and feeding it to a standalone copy of Llama-3.1-8B (Ultravox's backbone) with the same task prompts. We call this the implicit cascade: the model's own emergent text serves as the "transcript" for an independent LLM. If the implicit cascade's predictions match Ultravox's behavior, the text at audio positions is sufficient to explain the model's decisions. Table 6 shows that sufficiency depends on the task. On AG News, the implicit cascade achieves κ impl = 0.943 with Ultravox-higher than the agreement between the explicit Whisper cascade and Ultravox (κcasc = 0.933). This is despite only 34% bag precision: topic classification has a low information threshold, where a few keywords ("terrorism," "football," "stocks") suffice. The higher implicit agreement suggests that Ultravox's internal text reflects backbone-specific reasoning patterns rather than a generic transcript. Note that if layer 31 simply encoded the model's final answer, κ would be trivially ∼1.0 on all tasks; instead, the standalone Llama must reason over the decoded text anew. On SST-2 (κ = 0.14) and CSQA (κ = 0.25), the decoded text is insufficient: sentiment depends on negation and intensifiers easily lost in noisy decoding, and commonsense reasoning requires precise relational structure. MELD (κ = 0.15) serves as a negative control: emotion requires paralinguistic cues absent from any text representation.
Having established what is sufficient, we now test what is necessary.

div.head: LEACE Causal Erasure
div.p: The preceding analyses show that text representations emerge (logit lens) and can be sufficient (implicit cascade test). LEACE erasure tests whether they are causally necessary: does surgically removing text information collapse task performance?

We apply LEACE to both Ultravox and Qwen2-Audio (Table 7, Figure 6). Text erasure collapses both models to near-zero accuracy on every task (Ultravox 0.0-0.3%; Qwen2-Audio 0.0%), regardless of architecture. Random erasure of matched dimensionality has negligible effect on text-sufficient tasks (Ultravox AG News -4.0%, SST-2 -1.5%), confirming the collapse is text-specific. Text-predictive directions are causally necessary for task performance.

The more revealing finding concerns how each architecture encodes text. CTC and BoC probes both target text but capture different structure: CTC relies on frame-aligned character sequences, BoC on unordered character frequencies. Qwen2-Audio's cross-attention preserves frame-aligned structure from ). In short, each probe erases text only insofar as the architecture makes that structure linearly accessible. This maps onto the behavioral findings: Qwen2-Audio's frame-aligned encoding is structurally distinct from ASR output, explaining its lower κ; Ultravox's encoding crystallizes into transcript-like form by the final layers, explaining its higher κ. Finally, acoustic erasure (2D) causes unexpected accuracy drops even on text-sufficient tasks. A diagnostic reveals that in Qwen2-Audio, the acoustic eraser also damages text representations (TD drops by up to 0.25 at layer 8), confirming acoustic and text subspaces are entangled in cross-attention. In Ultravox, acoustic erasure does not affect text decodability (TD change < 0.03), suggesting it disrupts other processing rather than text itself. MELD drops under both random and acoustic erasure in both models, indicating fragile representations where any perturbation degrades performance; MELD-specific LEACE effects should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

div.head: Synthesis: Four Levels of Evidence
div.p: The mechanistic evidence forms a convergent chain: (i) Probing shows acoustic features are retained but compressed, while text decodability follows architecture-dependent trajectories (increasing for Ultravox, decreasing for Qwen2-Audio), answering what is encoded. (ii) Logit lens visualizes this as literal text emergence through the model's own vocabulary, answering how it emerges. (iii) Implicit transcript testing shows the emergent text is functionally sufficient for topic classification (κ=0.94) but not for fine-grained tasks (SST-2 κ=0.14, CSQA κ=0.25), establishing partial sufficiency that depends on information threshold. (iv) LEACE erasure confirms text representations are causally necessary in both architectures, with text erasure collapsing accuracy to near-zero; the architecturedependent pattern of CTC and BoC erasure reveals that how text is encoded determines how cascade-like the model behaves, establishing necessity.

The different logit lens trajectories explain the behav-ioral spectrum: Ultravox's progressive late-layer text emergence produces representations that closely resemble an explicit ASR transcript by the final layers, yielding higher cascade equivalence. Qwen2-Audio's cross-attention encoder already produces text-rich representations (CTC decodability ∼0.50 through layer 20) that the LLM sharply reorganizes in its final layers (0.29 at layer 31), yielding lower agreement even with matched backbones.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: When to use cascades vs. end-to-end models. Our results suggest a decision framework. For text-sufficient tasks in clean conditions, cascades are informationally equivalent to current speech LLMs, offering lower latency, cost, and engineering complexity, with independently upgradeable components. For noisy environments, our Whisper-based cascades prove more robust, losing only 0.5-4.2% at 0 dB SNR vs. 5.9-12.7% for the E2E models tested, though this advantage has been demonstrated with Whisper's noise-hardened front-end, it should generalize to most modern ASR systems given the widespread adoption of Whisper-adjacent modeling approaches. The case for E2E architectures rests on tasks with genuine acoustic surplus (emotion, sarcasm, speaker intent), but even there, probing reveals a gap between retaining and exploiting acoustic features.

Breaking cascade equivalence: a path forward. Our results identify the precise bottleneck: the models have the acoustic information but do not use it. Pitch and energy are retained through the final layers (R 2 > 0.29), yet erasing these directions barely affects Ultravox on natural-speech tasks (MELD -3.1%, MUStARD -4.0%). The problem is training incentive, not architectural capacity. Qwen2-Audio shows a larger effect from acoustic erasure (MELD -18.0%), suggesting its cross-attention architecture partially exploits acoustic information, consistent with its lower cascade equivalence and higher behavioral divergence from its cascade.

Three directions could break this bottleneck. First, paralinguistic auxiliary losses: a contrastive loss penalizing the model when acoustic features are predictable from text alone could encourage functionally independent acoustic channels. Architectures like WavLLM [6], which explicitly separate semantic and paralinguistic pathways, provide a structural foundation.

Second, minimal-pair prosodic training: training on audio pairs that differ only in prosody (e.g., sincere vs. sarcastic readings of the same sentence) could force models to attend to paralinguistic cues rather than defaulting to textual shortcuts. Building on contrastive objectives from self-supervised speech learning [32], a loss that pulls apart representations of prosodically distinct utterances with identical transcripts would directly target the textual bottleneck.
Third, architectural modality separation: cross-attention or dual-stream architectures that maintain a structurally independent acoustic pathway may be necessary for genuine multimodal reasoning.

Implications for benchmarking. Our findings show that comparing E2E speech LLMs against cascades requires controls that current evaluation practices lack: backbone matching to isolate architectural effects, per-example behavioral analysis beyond aggregate accuracy, and conditions that actually stress the audio pathway. A benchmark suite designed to reveal genuine architectural advantages should include: (1) to control for LLM reasoning differences. Without these controls, aggregate accuracy comparisons risk attributing backbone differences to architectural innovation.

Limitations. TTS-synthesized speech may underestimate acoustic surplus due to less natural prosody; acoustic erasure results corroborate this, showing larger effects on TTS tasks (Ultravox SST-2 -15.7%) than on natural-speech tasks (Ultravox MELD -3.1%). Both linear probes and LEACE operate in the linear subspace; nonlinearly encoded information would be invisible to both methods. Mechanistic analysis covers two of the four E2E models; Gemini is API-only, and Phi-4-MM was not probed due to its distinct architecture (Mixture-of-LoRAs with a separate conformer encoder), so the mechanistic conclusions may not generalize to all speech LLM designs.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented the first systematic test of whether speech LLMs are computationally equivalent to ASR→LLM cascades, combining matched-backbone behavioral testing with mechanistic evidence across two architectures. Our results reveal a spectrum: Ultravox is near-indistinguishable from its matched cascade on text-sufficient tasks, while Qwen2-Audio genuinely diverges. LEACE concept erasure confirms text representations are causally necessary in both architectures, collapsing accuracy to near-zero; the pattern of degradation further reveals that connector and cross-attention architectures encode text differently, explaining the behavioral spectrum. Under noise, our Whisper-based cascades prove substantially more robust than all E2E models tested.

Three takeaways for practitioners. First, evaluate with matched backbones: mismatched comparisons inflate apparent architectural differences and lead to incorrect conclusions about when end-to-end models add value. Second, use cascades as the default for text-sufficient tasks: they are informationally equivalent to current speech LLMs in clean conditions, cheaper to serve, and allow independent upgrades to the ASR or LLM component; with Whisper, they are also more noiserobust. Third, invest in end-to-end architectures only where acoustic surplus exists and can be exploited: current models re-tain paralinguistic features but fail to leverage them, suggesting that training objectives, not architectures, are the bottleneck.

Until training objectives reward direct exploitation of what audio uniquely provides, speech LLMs will remain implicit cascades, and teams building them should ask whether the modularity, robustness, and cost advantages of an explicit cascade are worth surrendering for architectural elegance that produces the same computation.
